questions.stem: A 57-year-old man presented with a lump on the right side of his neck. He had been feeling well with no systemic symptoms. He had well-controlled diabetes (HbA1C of 6%) and no drug allergies. On physical exam, the lump was nontender and easily moveable. It was not red or hot. He underwent a biopsy to evaluate for malignancy. Investigations: Direct microscopy: inflammatory cells and grampositive branching rods seen Culture: molar tooth-appearing colonies present on anaerobic plates
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Penicillin Microbiology and clinical presentation are consistent with infection by Actinomyces sp. Penicillin is the drug of choice for actinomycosis. Surgical resection is not typically necessary for Actinomyces cervicofacial infections unless there is a complex abscess or unless marsupialization of a fistula were required as antibiotics alone should be curative. If an empyema were present, drainage would be indicated. Doxycycline and clindamycin would be second-line agents and are reserved for cases where the patient has penicillin allergy. TMP–SMX would be used if treating Nocardia, but recall that Nocardia is an aerobic organism. Nocardia would be an unlikely organism in this location unless the patient had a penetrating trauma to the area.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q10

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man presented with a slow-growing painless soft tissue swelling of the perimandibular region over 2 months. It had started discharging small amounts of pus through a small opening in the skin 2 weeks earlier. It had responded temporarily to a short course of co-amoxiclav but had then relapsed. He had no weight loss, fever, chills, or other constitutional symptoms. He was otherwise in good health, worked in an office, and had a long-term male partner. He smoked 15 cigarettes a day. There was no history of recent dental work or trauma to the face or mouth. On examination there was a firm 4×5 cm mass in right submandibular region, tender to palpate, and partially fixed on the deep tissue planes. The overlying skin was slightly bluish in color, and there was a small sinus discharging thick yellow exudate. Investigations: CT head/neck: ill-defined mass in the left pyriform fossa involving the perimandibular gland and platysma muscle. Mass is infiltrative, crossing tissue planes. Moderately enhancing with several low attenuating foci. No associated lymphadenopathy A biopsy was performed: Direct microscopy: scanty gram-positive bacilli seen; branching filaments, diphtheroids, and coccobacilli Modified Kinyoun stain negative Bacterial cultures: aerobic, enhanced CO2 and anaerobic cultures negative Fungal cultures: no growth at 25°C or 37°C Histology: chronic inflammation with the presence of multiple granules surrounded by polymorphonuclear leukocytes; an eosinophilic fringe surrounds the PMN zone
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Actinomycosis Actinomycosis is most commonly caused by Actinomyces israelii, which may be a component of normal oropharyngeal flora. This chronic, invasive infection mimics malignancy as it may invade local muscle and bone if left untreated. Sinus tracts may occur. Oral cervicofacial actinomycosis is the commonest presentation, but thoracic and abdominopelvic infections are also seen. Diagnosis is usually by demonstration of gram-positive branching filamentous bacilli and sulfur granules; cultures are rarely positive if broad-spectrum antibiotics have been taken.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q50

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man is sent from otolaryngology clinic for evaluation of a chronic left mandibular wound. He has poor dentition and has had multiple tooth extractions. He has, for the last 2 months, had swelling and intermittently draining sinus tracts over the angle of his mandible. Superficial wound cultures have not grown any pathogens. Imaging does not show any signs of mandibular osteomyelitis.
questions.lead_in: First-line antimicrobial therapy for patients with this condition should include treatment with an agent in which of the following antibiotic classes?
questions.explanation: β-lactams Cervicofacial actinomycosis is most often treated with penicillins. A variety of other agents have been used with success, including cephalosporins, carbapenems, clindamycin, tetracyclines, erythromycin, and chloramphenicol.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q38

questions.question: A woman has an IUD and presents with fever, chronic abdominal pain, and malodorous vaginal discharge. A gram stain is shown. CT shows a pelvic mass. [image-based question: gram stain]

parts.text: What is the diagnosis?
What do you recommend the gynecologist immediately do?
What is the initial treatment? Name the drug and route.
What is the duration of the treatment?
If a woman with an IUD has the same gram stain but is asymptomatic, what should be done?

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: PID +/- tubo-ovarian abscess, possibly pelvic actinomycosis pending culture. Immediate: Remove the IUD, surgical removal of mass vs IR aspirate with culture. Initial treatment: Empiric CRO 1g IV daily + doxycycline 100mg BID + metronidazole 500mg BID until well enough for oral stepdown, then metro/doxy for 14 days total, plus actino treatment (amoxil or penicillin, technically IV for 14 days then PO stepdown); actino specific: IV PenG x2 weeks then 6-12 months PO. Asymptomatic: counsel and monitor for symptoms, IUD stays in.

questions.question: 26. Patient has a tooth extraction then returns months later with a small abscess in the submandibular area. Gram stain shows branching GPB.

parts.text: What is the organism (species and genus)? (0.5)
What findings would there be on pathology? (0.5)
What is the initial treatment for this? (0.5)

cohort_answer.text: Actinomyces israelii (most common) - grows on routine agar, characteristic molar tooth colony. Pathology: Sulfur granules comprised of delicate branching filaments of Actinomyces, surrounded by inflammatory cells. Treatment: Penicillin 3-4 million U IV q8h or Amoxicillin 500mg PO q6h; alternatives Doxycycline 100mg IV/PO q12h, Clindamycin 900mg IV q8h or 300-450mg PO q6h

questions.question: 37yo F with IUD in situ with 2 year history of chronic pelvic pain and Pap showing beaded GP bacilli and sulfur granules on biopsy (shown picture). CT shows endometritis and adnexal mass.

parts.text: What is the clinical syndrome
What should the gynecologist do
What is your antibiotic choice including route
What is your duration of antibiotic treatment
What if the patient was asymptomatic but had the same gram stain findings on Pap?

questions.model_answer:
a) Clinical syndrome: pelvic actinomycosis (IUD-associated), a tissue-invasive Actinomyces infection with an inflammatory pelvic/tubo-ovarian mass — beaded gram-positive branching bacilli with sulfur granules are characteristic.
b) Gynecologist should remove the IUD (source of infection) and obtain tissue/cultures to confirm diagnosis; drain/debride the adnexal abscess if needed (surgery may be required for a large mass not responding to antibiotics, though extensive surgery should be avoided if possible since disease usually resolves with prolonged antibiotics once the IUD is removed).
c) Antibiotic choice: high-dose intravenous penicillin G, then transition to oral penicillin (or amoxicillin) once clinically improved.
d) Duration: prolonged course, typically 6–12 months total (weeks of IV therapy followed by months of oral therapy) to ensure eradication given the tendency for actinomycosis to relapse.
e) If asymptomatic with the same Pap findings: Actinomyces-like organisms are found incidentally on Pap smear in 4–8% of IUD users and do not equate to invasive pelvic actinomycosis; no antibiotic treatment or IUD removal is required — observe/monitor for symptoms.
questions.beyond_mandell: Specific antibiotic dose/duration for tissue-invasive pelvic actinomycosis (high-dose IV penicillin G followed by 6-12 months oral penicillin/amoxicillin) reflects standard actinomycosis treatment guidance rather than text explicitly present in this chapter excerpt.

questions.question: PM 24. Lady with an IUD, pelvic pain and foul vaginal discharge growing GPB branching bacilli on swab, picture shown (large clump of blue GPB). [image-based question: gram stain of branching GPB]

parts.text: What is the diagnosis? (1)
What do you tell the OB to do immediately (1)
What one antibiotic to give with route (1)
If someone else has an IUD with GBP and is asymptomatic what would you recommend (1)

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: Actinomyces israelii infection. Immediate action: Remove IUD, do pelvic US looking for abscess. Antibiotic: Ampicillin or Pen G (IV). Asymptomatic with ALOs: Part of normal flora - removal of IUD unnecessary unless causing disease (ALOs seen in ~7% of Pap smears in IUCD users; low PPV for pelvic infection; warrants patient education and follow-up, not removal, unless equally suitable contraception can be agreed on).

questions.question: Young girl with copper IUD, 2 years of pelvic pain and now evidence of endometritis, adnexal mass, and peripelvic inflammation.

parts.text: What is the diagnosis?
What should the gynecologist do imminently?
What initial treatment regimen?
What is the recommended duration of treatment?
In an alternative patient, what to do with IUD if asymptomatic and this organism is identified on pap smear?

questions.model_answer:
a) Diagnosis: pelvic actinomycosis (associated with long-term copper IUD use), caused by Actinomyces israelii.
b) Imminent gynecologic step: remove the IUD and send it (plus any tissue/pus obtained) for culture and histopathology to confirm the diagnosis; assess for abscess requiring drainage.
c) Initial treatment regimen: high-dose intravenous penicillin G.
d) Recommended duration: prolonged therapy - IV penicillin for 2-6 weeks followed by oral penicillin (or amoxicillin) to complete a total of 6-12 months.
e) Asymptomatic patient with Actinomyces on Pap smear: remove the IUD; antibiotics are generally not required if the patient remains asymptomatic (monitor clinically; treat only if symptoms develop).

questions.question: Woman with endometriosis and endometritis stemming from and IUD. Gram + rods on staining. CT shows an adnexal inflammatory mass. Showed an image with clue cells.

parts.text: Asked for the diagnosis
What you would do for this patient immediately?
Antibiotic Route
Total duration of therapy
Asked what treatment would be indicated if this were uncomplicated

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: PID +/- tubo-ovarian complex/abscess (polymicrobial, often including Gardnerella); clue cells suggest BV, particularly Gardnerella vaginalis. Immediate action: Beta-HCG to rule out ectopic pregnancy; Chlamydia + gonorrhoeae NAAT prior to Rx, screen for other STIs including HIV; empiric Rx. Abx route/regimen: Cefoxitin 2g IV q6h + Doxycycline 100mg IV BID + Metronidazole 500mg PO BID (alternatives: Clindamycin+gentamicin, Ofloxacin+Metronidazole, Levofloxacin+Metronidazole, Amp/Sulbactam+Doxycycline, Cipro+Doxy+metronidazole); outpatient CTX 250mg IM x1 + doxycycline 100mg PO BID x14d +/- flagyl if BV; inpatient Cefotetan 2g IV q12h OR cefoxitin 2g IV q6h + doxycycline. Duration: 14 days if uncomplicated (up to 4-6 weeks for TOA). Uncomplicated treatment: Ceftriaxone 250mg IM x1 + Doxycycline x14d OR Cefoxitin 2g IM x1 + Probenecid 1g PO x1 + Doxycycline x14d (add flagyl given clue cells/BV)

questions.question: Woman with copper IUD has Pap smear, it shows [picture of messy Gram-positive bacilli]. She has several months of pelvic pain and probably other symptoms too.

parts.text: What is the most likely diagnosis?
What do you recommend that the Gynecologist does?
What is your initial antimicrobial therapy? Include the name and route.
What is the total duration of treatment?
What would you do if the same findings on pap smear were found in a different woman who had a copper IUD but no symptoms?

questions.model_answer:
a) Most likely diagnosis: pelvic actinomycosis (Actinomyces israelii) associated with prolonged copper IUD use.
b) Recommend the gynecologist remove the IUD and obtain tissue/culture to confirm the diagnosis, assessing for a pelvic abscess requiring drainage.
c) Initial antimicrobial therapy: high-dose penicillin G, intravenous route.
d) Total duration of treatment: 6-12 months (IV penicillin for the initial 2-6 weeks, transitioning to oral penicillin or amoxicillin to complete the course).
e) If the same Pap smear finding is seen in an asymptomatic woman with a copper IUD: remove the IUD; no antibiotic treatment is necessary if she remains asymptomatic.

questions.question: A man had a tooth resected 4 weeks ago. He presents with a 3-week history of worsening pain and swelling at the site of his extraction. On examination, he has a small submandibular mass. Aspirate is performed, with gram stain demonstrating gram positive bacilli.

parts.text: What is the organism (to genus-level)?
What other feature would you expect to find on histopathology?
What would be your first-line treatment?

questions.model_answer:
a) Organism (genus level): Actinomyces.
b) Additional histopathologic feature expected: sulfur granules (yellow-white granules composed of filamentous organism aggregates, often surrounded by the Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon/eosinophilic material).
c) First-line treatment: high-dose penicillin G (initially IV), followed by a prolonged course of oral penicillin or amoxicillin.

questions.question: Child who had a dental procedure and developed facial mass from the dental site. Biopsy showed branching GPB.

parts.text: What is the name of the bacteria genus
What is one additional finding you may see on pathology?
What is the preferred treatment?

questions.model_answer:
a) Bacterial genus: Actinomyces.
b) Additional pathology finding: sulfur granules (basophilic/yellow granules of clustered filamentous organisms, may show the Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon).
c) Preferred treatment: high-dose penicillin G (IV), followed by prolonged oral penicillin or amoxicillin (total duration typically several months).

parts.text: Name of organism
Path finding
Treatment (just name it)

cohort_answer.text:
Name: Actinomyces israelii - GPB, branching, anaerobic, not acid-fast.
Path finding: Sulphur granules.
Treatment: Actinomyces alone - if serious/bulky disease: IV PenG 18-24 MU x4-6 weeks then PO Amox or Pen VK 6-12 months (Mandell, UTD). If mild: Pen VK or Amox x2-6 months, aiming for clinical resolution to prevent relapse. Given commonly polymicrobial, may want to broaden coverage with Amox/Clav (UTD). Alternate therapies: clindamycin, tetracyclines.

questions.question: Middle aged guy has chronic history of swelling, and drainage of the face after prior tooth extraction. Sinus tract noted. Aspirate shows GPB

parts.text: Most likely pathogen (down to genus) (0.5)
What else are you likely to see on pathology (0.5)
What empiric antibiotic do you start (0.5)

cohort_answer.text: Pathogen: Actinomyces. Pathology: Sulfur granules. Empiric antibiotic: IV penicillin G (if oral involvement could go with IV Clavulin; if not severe could consider oral penicillin or clavulin). Additional notes: Chronic infection often mimics malignancy and can be related to IUD infection; susceptible to penicillin, alternatives tetracyclines, clindamycin, less evidence but potentially ceftriaxone, imipenem; treatment usually 2-6 weeks IV followed by 6-12 months oral; drainage of collections, surgery for CNS or refractory disease

questions.question: Q92 2023 Day 2. [image-based question: photomicrographs/stains shown with a sporotrichoid spread pattern; 4 different images shown and the candidate is asked to identify the organism for each]

parts.text: Identify the organism shown in image 1 (H&E stain)
Identify the organism shown in image 2 (branching gram-positive rods)
Identify the organism shown in image 3 (tiny gram-negative coccobacilli, no growth on MacConkey)
Identify the organism shown in image 4 (PAS stain with budding yeast-like cells and conidiophores)

cohort_answer.text:
Image 1: Leishmania spp. amastigotes, H&E stain - spherical to ovoid, 1-5 µm long by 1-2 µm wide, large nucleus, prominent kinetoplast, short axoneme (rarely visible by light microscopy); reside in macrophages.
Image 2: Nocardia - branching, filamentous, beaded, gram-positive rods with right angle branching (compare/contrast with Rhodococcus equi).
Image 3: Francisella tularensis - tiny, gram-negative coccobacilli, no growth on MacConkey; 'junky' gram stain of tiny GNCB's, DDx Francisella or Brucella; oxidase negative, urease negative, weakly catalase positive, strict aerobes.
Image 4: Sporothrix schenckii - small (~2 microns); PAS stained tissue section showing budding yeast-like cells; conidiophores and conidia are ovoid, elongated, 3-6 x 2-3 µm, one-celled, smooth walled, hyaline.

questions.question: A 51 year-old man, on dexamethasone for a glioblastoma, is admitted with fever and progressively worsening respiratory symptoms x 18 days. CT chest shows multiple non-cavitary nodules measuring 1.5 to 5 cm. Placed on piperacillin/tazobactam and ciprofloxacin, but continues to worsen despite this treatment. After 4 days, respiratory cultures grow dry, yellow colonies. Beaded, filamentous Gram-positive rods are seen on Gram stain.

parts.text: a) What is the pathogen?
b) What is the most important next test?
c) What are three other Gram-positive rods that can grow aerobically that can cause a similar clinical picture?

cohort_answer.text:
a) What is the pathogen? - Nocardia spp
b) What is the most important next test? - Modified Acid fast staining - main DDx = Actinomyces which does not stain with modified acid fast but nocardia does (CT head if you already have identified the pathogen) [source note: Uptodate]
c) What are three other Gram-positive rods that can grow aerobically that can cause a similar clinical picture? - Rhodococcus, Gordonia, Tsukumeullea, Streptomyces - also GPB but not pathogenic so wouldn't include in this answer but FYI
cohort_answer.source: AB 2019 (answer slides (with Gram stain and Acid-Fast Staining images interspersed); speaker notes citing Uptodate for part b)
